title: Giving an AI agent the keys to Business Central: practical security tips.
summary: Securing AI agents that act on data in Business Central requires deliberate choices about identity, permissions, validation and oversight. The post provides a framework for deploying agents safely using existing tools like MFA, least privilege and change control, ensuring accountability stays with people rather than the agent.
key_points: AI agents need their own application identity with narrow permissions built from the task backwards, not shared logins or broad service accounts
Treat all data the agent reads (PDFs, emails, fields) as untrusted input vulnerable to prompt injection and validate it with deterministic code before acting
Require human approval with full evidence (source documents, matched orders, rule violations, agent identity) and enforce posting rights so only humans can finalize records
Plan for failure before go-live: rehearse disabling the agent, audit trails to trace what it did, and point-in-time restore capability to repair damage
AI-generated code in development must follow normal engineering gates (branch policies, analyzers, human review) and avoid closed-loop approval by multiple AI systems
features: Permission sets and role-based access control

quotes.text: The agent can do the work, but accountability stays with people.
quotes.why_it_matters: Summarizes the core principle: agents execute but humans remain responsible, preventing delegation of accountability

quotes.text: Permitted, plausible and wrong is the failure mode to design against.
quotes.why_it_matters: Highlights that technical permissions alone cannot prevent incorrect decisions; additional controls and human judgment are required

quotes.text: These checks are boring, testable and impossible to sweet-talk, which is exactly what you want from a control.
quotes.why_it_matters: Emphasizes that deterministic validation rules are more reliable than trusting the agent's judgment to follow instructions
